vocab.title: Match each word to its precise meaning
defs: to place two things side by side so that their differences stand out
so strong or real that it can almost be touched
gently filled or spread through, usually with light, color or feeling
bringing strong images, memories or feelings to mind
a vivid written or spoken description of a work of visual art
to fill something deeply with a quality, feeling or idea
the position from which you see something, or the way you see it
to undermine an expectation or convention, often quietly and on purpose

reading.rtitle: The Weight of a Thin Stream of Milk
paras: Most visitors give The Milkmaid about as long as it takes to read its label. The painting is small, barely larger than a sheet of newspaper, and it hangs in the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam among canvases that are far louder about their own importance. What it offers instead is an act so ordinary that the eye is tempted to slide past it: a kitchen maid pouring milk into an earthenware bowl. Stay a little longer, however, and the modesty of the subject begins to feel less like an absence of ambition than a deliberate choice.

Very little in the picture is there to decorate it. The wall behind the woman is austere, bare plaster interrupted only by a nail and the faint shadow that the nail casts. Vermeer could have filled that space with a map, a mirror or a view through a doorway, as many of his contemporaries routinely did. His refusal to do so is what makes the picture arresting. With so little to distract us, our attention has nowhere to go but to the woman, the table and the light that falls across both from the window on the left.

That light is the true subject of the painting. The corner of the room is suffused with it, cool and even, the kind of northern daylight that reveals texture rather than drama. The bread on the table is rendered in a scatter of tiny raised dots of paint, so that the crust seems to catch and hold the light instead of merely reflecting it. The blue of the apron, made from one of the most expensive pigments a painter could buy, is almost luminous against the yellow of the bodice. Vermeer juxtaposes the rough surfaces of basket and crust with the smooth glaze of the jug, and the contrast makes each material more palpable than it would be on its own.

It is the thin stream of milk, though, that holds the whole composition together. It is the only thing in the painting that moves, and it is painted with such meticulous care that we can almost measure its pace. The woman's concentration is total. Her eyes are lowered and her arms are held with the steadiness of someone who knows that a spill would waste something precious. The effect is quietly evocative: a single second has been stretched into something closer to a vow.

Paintings of kitchen maids were not unusual in the Dutch Republic of the seventeenth century. Many of them, however, came with a wink. The maid was a stock figure of comedy or temptation, and the viewer was invited to judge her. Vermeer subverts that convention without announcing that he is doing so. There is no joke here and no moral lesson, only a working woman imbued with a dignity that the genre had rarely allowed her. His handling of the scene is restrained rather than sentimental, and that restraint is precisely what lets the viewer arrive at respect instead of being instructed to feel it.

The vantage point matters too. We look at the woman from slightly below, the way one might look up at a statue, and her figure fills the frame with a solidity that has little to do with her size. Critics have sometimes called the painting a tableau, but the word suggests a pose held for an audience, and the milkmaid is not performing for anyone. She is simply working, and the picture asks us to notice what that work requires.

This is where ekphrasis, the practice of describing a work of art in words, becomes more than an exercise. To describe The Milkmaid well is to slow down enough to see why it was made the way it was. A list of objects will not do it. The description has to account for the choices behind them: the empty wall, the dotted bread, the lowered eyes. Looking, in the end, is a discipline before it is a pleasure, and this small painting rewards anyone willing to practice it.

gist.prompt: Which statement best captures the writer's central claim?
choices: The painting is admired mainly because Vermeer could afford an unusually expensive blue pigment.
The painting's apparent modesty is the result of deliberate choices that reward slow, attentive looking.
Dutch paintings of kitchen maids were mostly comic, and The Milkmaid is the most successful joke among them.

items: The writer implies that the small scale of the painting is a limitation Vermeer never managed to overcome.
The text says the modesty of the subject feels 'less like an absence of ambition than a deliberate choice'. Scale is presented as a decision, not a failure.
According to the writer, the emptiness of the wall intensifies our focus on the figure.
'With so little to distract us, our attention has nowhere to go but to the woman, the table and the light.'
The writer characterizes the light in the painting as theatrical.
The light is 'cool and even, the kind of northern daylight that reveals texture rather than drama'. Theatrical is the opposite claim.
Vermeer's treatment of the maid departs from the way the genre typically portrayed such women.
Other maids 'came with a wink' and invited judgment; 'Vermeer subverts that convention'.
The writer wholeheartedly endorses calling the painting a tableau.
'The word suggests a pose held for an audience, and the milkmaid is not performing for anyone.' The writer questions the label.

parts: For almost two centuries after his death in 1675, Vermeer was a name that meant little outside a small circle of collectors.
Several of his pictures had even been sold under the names of better-known painters.
It was a French critic writing in the 1860s who argued, with the zeal of a convert, that these scattered canvases were the work of a single and singular master.
His campaign took years, and not everyone was persuaded at first.
Part of the difficulty was simple scarcity: fewer than forty paintings are now attributed to him.
He seems to have worked slowly and never to have run a large workshop that could multiply his output.
That scarcity has shaped how we look at him ever since. Every surviving picture carries the weight of the ones that were never painted, or never found.
It is hard to stand in front of one without wondering what else was lost.

items.situation: Upgrade this sentence: "The light in the painting is really nice."
tips: The corner of the room is suffused with a cool, even light.
Say what the light does to the room, not how you feel about it.

items.situation: Upgrade this sentence: "The wall is kind of empty and boring."
tips: The austerity of the wall keeps our attention on the figure.
Turn the adjective into a noun and let the noun make the argument.

items.situation: Upgrade this sentence: "He put the rough bread next to the shiny jug."
tips: He juxtaposes the rough crust with the smooth glaze of the jug.
Name the two surfaces precisely before you name the contrast.

items.situation: Upgrade this sentence: "The maid looks very focused on what she is doing."
tips: One noun can replace an entire clause, and it sounds more certain.

items.situation: Upgrade this sentence: "He didn't turn her into a joke like other painters did."
tips: He subverts the comic convention of the genre.
Name the convention first, then say what he did to it.

items.situation: Upgrade this sentence: "It makes you feel a lot of stuff."
tips: Evocative needs no intensifier. Very evocative is weaker, not stronger.

listenings.text: Welcome to stop fourteen, the smallest painting in this gallery and, for many visitors, the one they remember longest. Johannes Vermeer painted The Milkmaid around 1658, when he was still in his twenties and still working out what kind of painter he wanted to be. Before you read anything else, take a moment simply to look. Notice where the light comes from. It enters through the window on the left and settles on the woman's face, on her arms and on the bread on the table. Now step a little closer and look at the crust of that bread. Those tiny raised dots are not an accident. Vermeer placed them one by one, so that the surface would seem to glitter. The blue of her apron was made from one of the most expensive pigments a painter could buy, which tells you how seriously he took this humble scene. Finally, look at the wall behind her. It is almost empty. Vermeer chose to leave it that way, and that emptiness is doing more work than any decoration could. When you are ready, please continue to stop fifteen.

Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Introduction to Art History. Before we look at a single slide this semester, I want to tell you what this course will actually ask of you, because it is not what most of you expect. You probably think the hard part is memorizing names and dates. It is not. The hard part is describing what you see so precisely that someone who has never seen the work could imagine it. That practice has an old name, ekphrasis, and it is the foundation of everything we will do together. Your first assignment is due next Thursday. Choose one painting in the university museum, stand in front of it for at least twenty minutes, and then write six hundred words about it. There are two rules. You may not use the words beautiful, amazing or interesting, and you may not look anything up before you write. I want your eyes, not the internet's. Most of you will find the first ten minutes unbearably slow. Stay anyway. That is exactly the moment when you start to see.
